page_hint: Ch 12 §8 mini-case, economics paragraph
quoted_clause: "i.e. ~$232.2K self-host and ~$467.2K cloud-equivalent from the same component rates — per-host capex + energy plus a fixed ~$10K/mo staff component (Ch 16)"
observed: The cloud-equivalent at 32 hosts is exactly 32 × $14,600 = $467,200, i.e. a pure per-host figure with no staff component, whereas the self-host figure is 32 × $6,943.66 + $10,000 = $232,197. The phrase 'from the same component rates' therefore does not hold for the cloud leg, and the reader cannot tell whether the staff component is inside or outside the cloud number.
evidence: 21 × $14,600 = $306,600 ✓ (the 21-host cloud figure); 6 × $14,600 = $87,600 ✓ (the 'default paid-occupancy input', i.e. the 6-host average-load fleet — this is not stated anywhere); (155,816.93 − 10,000)/21 = $6,943.66/host; 32 × 6,943.66 + 10,000 = $232,197 ✓.
root_cause: Two cost models (self-host with a fixed staff component; cloud as pure per-host) are described as sharing 'the same component rates'.
correction: State the composition of each leg explicitly (self-host = per-host capex + energy + $10K/mo staff; cloud = per-host rental only, staff excluded or included and stated), and label the $87,600 figure's basis (6 hosts at the average-load screen).
acceptance_test: Each of the three cost figures ($155,816.93, $232.2K, $467.2K) has its composition printed, and the $87,600 figure's host count is stated.

page_hint: Ch 12 Table 12-1 (memory column note); Ch 13 §3 'Placing the Canonical Workload'

page_hint: Ch 12 §1 Concept; §8 mini-case; Ch 13 §3 'Escalating'
quoted_clause: Ch 12 §1: "the three gates this chapter fixes"; Ch 12 mini-case: "the chapter notes it equals one host's cloud-equivalent"; Ch 13: "continuous batching on 8×H100 at ~9.5K tokens/request sustained roughly tens of thousands of tokens/s"

evidence: Ch 12 §3 and Table 12-2 both state ~19,800 tok/s per host; Ch 13 §3 uses 'tens of thousands' instead.
root_cause: Loose editing; a precise number was replaced by an approximation in one place.

page_hint: Ch15 §6 (Architecture Consequence), paragraph beginning 'These choices together would change the basis of the throughput figure'
quoted_clause: ~35,000–48,000 tokens/s [ILLUSTRATIVE achievable range] at the canonical context (with flash, continuous batch; a mixed prefill+decode aggregate; upper end = the case-(ii) attention-adjusted ceiling, lower end = the mini-case's per-host figure) ... the single-host upper end is capped by the 100%-MFU parameter-matmul-only ceiling: 7.91×10¹⁵ FLOP/s ÷ 1.4×10¹¹ FLOP/token ≈ 56,500 tok/s under the linear-only case (i) — a 2N-only figure; at the canonical 9,200-token context the attention term (§3, case ii) lowers this to ≈48,000 tok/s (≈52,000 under the causal case (iii)) — so the illustrative range is ~35,000–48,000 at canonical context
observed: The per-host throughput range is internally inconsistent with the chapter's own numbers on three separate bases, and its label ('achievable range') contradicts its own construction. (a) The upper end, 48,000 tok/s, is by construction the 100%-MFU ceiling (7.912e15 FLOP/s ÷ 1.6412e11 FLOP/token = 48,208), i.e. a theoretical maximum that no system attains; calling the range 'achievable' re-introduces exactly the MFU>1 error the chapter spends a paragraph forbidding. (b) The lower end, 35,000 tok/s/host, implies 35,000 × 1.4e11 = 4.90e15 FLOP/s ÷ 7.912e15 = 61.9% MFU under case (i) (72.6% under case (ii)), which contradicts §3's own 35% MFU planning screen (7.912e15 × 0.35 ÷ 1.4e11 = 19,779 tok/s/host) by a factor of ~1.8×. (c) The label 'mixed prefill+decode aggregate' is not supportable: at the canonical 9,500-token context the host's decode-bandwidth ceiling is ≈809 tok/s (see CH15-02), so a 35,000 tok/s aggregate is ≥97.7% prefill — it is a prefill rate, not a mixed rate. (d) 35,000 tok/s/host ÷ 9,200 tok/req = 3.80 rps/host, which contradicts §4's own '~2 rps per host' admission capacity (17 slots ÷ 8.6 s = 1.98 rps) by ~1.9×.
root_cause: The chapter mixes three incompatible bases inside one quoted range — a theoretical 100%-MFU ceiling, an achievable mixed-workload rate, and a per-host figure imported from another chapter's mini-case — and then labels the union 'achievable'. The 35% planning screen established in §3 is never carried forward to §6, so the two efficiency assumptions (35% vs ~62–73%) coexist without reconciliation.
correction: Split the statement into three explicitly labelled quantities: (i) the 100%-MFU prefill ceiling (56,500 case (i) / 48,000 case (ii) / 52,000 case (iii)) labelled as a theoretical bound, not an achievable rate; (ii) the planning-screen rate implied by §3's 35% MFU (≈19,800 tok/s/host case (i)); (iii) the mini-case's per-host figure, with its workload level and MFU assumption stated and reconciled against (ii). If a single range is retained, label it 'illustrative planning range' and state the MFU assumption behind each endpoint; do not call a 100%-MFU ceiling 'achievable'. Also drop or qualify 'mixed prefill+decode aggregate' unless the decode share is computed.
acceptance_test: A reader can state, for each of the three numbers (56,500 / 48,000 / 35,000), its FLOP/token convention, its implied MFU, and whether it is a bound or an estimate; and can verify that no number in the range is labelled 'achievable' while being equal to a 100%-MFU ceiling. The 35,000 tok/s/host figure is either reconciled with §3's 35% screen or explicitly flagged as resting on a different (stated) efficiency assumption.

page_hint: Ch15 §3 (Worked Example), paragraph beginning 'The architectural conclusion, that there is no single bottleneck for the whole request, stands'
quoted_clause: At the canonical peak, prefill shows a *workload capacity deficit* — aggregate compute demand above the host's peak (it needs more FLOPs/s than the host can supply, and leans on caching/queueing). Decode is primarily memory-bandwidth constrained, and maximum concurrency is constrained by KV residency. Each phase is established from arithmetic intensity and the roofline (Chapter 8), never from an impossible "MFU > 1."
observed: The chapter promises a phase-by-phase establishment and delivers it for prefill (a demand/peak ratio of ~6.5×) but not for decode. Decode is asserted to be 'primarily memory-bandwidth constrained' with no demand/peak ratio at all, even though the chapter has already computed every input needed (140 GB weights, 24.9 GB KV per 9,500-token sequence, 12,000 output tok/s peak demand, 17-slot KV-limited concurrency). The natural completion is bytes/token = weights/B + KV_bytes = 140/B + 24.9 GB: at B = 17 that is 33.1 GB/token, so 12,000 tok/s demands ≈398 TB/s against a host peak of 8 × 3.35 TB/s = 26.8 TB/s — a ~14.8× deficit; even as B → ∞ the KV term alone (24.9 GB/token) gives 299 TB/s, a ~11× deficit. The per-host decode ceiling is therefore ≈809 tok/s, so decode alone needs ≈15 hosts at the theoretical bandwidth limit — comparable to the 19-host prefill screen. The 19-host screen is thus prefill-only and is presented as if it were the fleet answer. The same omission also hides prefill's KV-write traffic (368,000 tok/s × 2.62144 MB = 965 GB/s, ≈3.6% of host peak) and the fact that the decode FLOP ratio of 0.21 (§3) says nothing about decode headroom, because decode is not FLOP-limited.
evidence: Recomputed: KV per sequence = 9,500 × 2,621,440 B = 24.90 GB; weights = 70e9 × 2 B = 140 GB; host HBM peak (H100 SXM) = 8 × 3.35 TB/s = 26.8 TB/s; bytes/token at B=17 = 140/17 + 24.90 = 33.14 GB; 12,000 × 33.14 GB = 397.7 TB/s → 14.8× over peak; per-host ceiling = 26,800 GB/s ÷ 33.14 GB = 809 tok/s; 12,000/809 = 14.8 hosts. Cross-check against the chunk's own §4 figure: 2 rps/host × 300 tok = 600 decode tok/s vs the 809 ceiling (74% duty) and 2 × 9,200 = 18,400 prefill tok/s vs §3's 35%-screen rate of 19,779 tok/s — §3 and §4 are mutually consistent, which confirms the missing decode check is the only gap.
root_cause: The chapter's analytical template (demand ÷ peak, per phase) was applied to prefill's FLOP axis but not to decode's bandwidth axis, even though decode's binding resource is bandwidth and the chapter says so. The omission is then masked by the 0.21 FLOP ratio, which is on the wrong axis for decode.
correction: Add the decode demand/peak check to §3, immediately after the prefill one, using the same template: bytes/token = W/B + KV_bytes_per_token; demand = 12,000 × bytes/token; compare with 8 × HBM bandwidth. State the resulting per-host decode ceiling and the implied host count for the decode phase, and state explicitly that the 19-host screen is prefill-derived and must be combined with (not substituted for) the decode requirement. Add the prefill KV-write term (965 GB/s) for completeness. Also state the H100 variant (SXM 3.35 TB/s vs PCIe 2.0 TB/s) since the result depends on it.
acceptance_test: §3 contains a decode-phase demand/peak ratio computed on the bandwidth axis, with the batch size stated, and the text no longer presents the prefill-derived host count as the fleet answer without noting the decode requirement. A reader can reproduce the decode host count from the chapter's own inputs.

page_hint: Ch15 §4 (Measurement), paragraph beginning 'On the FlashAttention "traffic reduction" claim, be precise about the units'
quoted_clause: That is a *rate*, not a byte count — FlashAttention finishes sooner, so a higher achieved rate over a shorter run still yields fewer total bytes per request.
observed: The inference is invalid as stated. Bytes transferred = achieved rate × elapsed time. A higher achieved rate over a shorter run yields fewer bytes only if the speed-up exceeds the rate ratio; with the chapter's own illustrative numbers (400 GB/s vs 150 GB/s, a 2.67× rate ratio) the byte totals are equal only if FlashAttention finishes 2.67× sooner, and are otherwise ambiguous. The sentence asserts a general implication that does not hold, and it is immediately followed by the correct statement ('A bandwidth figure alone does not establish that fewer bytes/request were transferred'), so the paragraph contradicts itself. The byte reduction is real, but it follows from the mechanism (no materialized L×L intermediate), not from the rate comparison.
evidence: bytes = rate × time. With rate_1 = 400 GB/s, rate_0 = 150 GB/s, bytes_1 < bytes_0 requires t_0/t_1 > 400/150 = 2.67. The chapter supplies no such bound. The correct causal chain is: no materialized intermediate → fewer bytes per request (mechanism) → shorter runtime → higher achieved rate (consequence), not the reverse.
root_cause: The paragraph is trying to correct a units error (rate vs byte count) and over-corrects into a false implication, because the author did not separate 'the mechanism reduces bytes' from 'the measurement shows a higher rate'.
correction: Rewrite as: 'A bandwidth figure is a rate, not a byte count: bytes = rate × time, so a higher achieved rate over a shorter run does not by itself establish fewer bytes. The byte reduction follows from the mechanism — the materialized L×L intermediate is not written and re-read — and must be confirmed as bytes/request (or read/write transaction counters) under a matched workload.'
acceptance_test: The paragraph contains no sentence in which a rate comparison is used to conclude a byte reduction; the causal direction runs mechanism → bytes → runtime → rate.

page_hint: Ch15 §3 (Worked Example), paragraph beginning 'Compute demand versus peak — and why this is not an MFU'
quoted_clause: The decode figure at 12,000 tokens/s is ≈ 1.68 ×10¹⁵ ÷ 7.91 ×10¹⁵ ≈ 0.21, i.e. ~21 % — again a groundable number, not a ceiling-defying one; the actual achieved value must come from the target serving benchmark.
observed: The paragraph's whole purpose is to separate a demand ratio from an achieved MFU, and it does so correctly for prefill ('What it must not be called is "MFU = 6.5"'). The decode sentence then abandons that discipline: 'again a groundable number' invites the reader to treat 21% as an achieved MFU, and the ratio is presented without the label 'demand'. Worse, a sub-1.0 FLOP ratio for decode is easy to misread as evidence of decode headroom, when decode is bandwidth- and KV-limited and the FLOP axis is not the binding constraint (see CH15-02, where the decode bandwidth deficit is ~15×). The chapter's own opening paragraph warns against exactly this collapse ('whether either phase is actually compute- or bandwidth-bound is a property of the model × workload × kernel × hardware operating point'), so the unqualified 'Decode is primarily memory-bandwidth constrained' later in the same section also undercuts its own caveat.
evidence: 12,000 × 1.4e11 = 1.68e15; 1.68e15/7.912e15 = 0.2123. The ratio is a demand/peak ratio on the FLOP axis. Decode's binding axis is bandwidth: 12,000 tok/s × 33.1 GB/token (B=17) = 398 TB/s vs 26.8 TB/s peak (CH15-02).
root_cause: The demand/achieved distinction was established once and then not applied consistently; the decode ratio was written as a 'figure' rather than as a labelled demand ratio on a named axis.
correction: Label the decode number explicitly as a demand-to-peak ratio on the FLOP axis, e.g. 'the decode FLOP demand is ≈21% of the host's FP16 peak — a demand ratio on the compute axis, not an achieved MFU, and not evidence of decode headroom, because decode is limited by bytes/token (bandwidth) and by KV residency, not by FLOPs.' Then add the bandwidth-axis ratio (CH15-02).
acceptance_test: Every ratio in §3 is explicitly labelled as demand-vs-peak or achieved, and states which resource axis it is on. No reader can arrive at 'decode has 79% headroom' from the text.

page_hint: Ch15 §5 (Common Mistakes), third bullet, 'Using scaled-dot-product attention without FlashAttention'
quoted_clause: and it pays off specifically when memory-bound; for moderate lengths (2,000–4,000 tokens) the HBM bandwidth reduction can translate to a ~1.3–1.8× throughput gain on H100 (illustrative — bench the specific kernel on the target hardware)
observed: The referent of 'throughput gain' is unstated (attention-kernel throughput vs end-to-end request throughput), and the number is not derivable from either reading using the chapter's own arithmetic. End-to-end: the chapter computes in §3 that attention is ≈15% of total forward FLOPs at 9,200 tokens; at 2,000–4,000 tokens the same formula gives attention = 4·80·L²·8192 / (2·70e9·L + 4·80·L²·8192) = 3.7% (L=2,000) and 7.5% (L=4,000) of total FLOPs, so even a free attention kernel bounds the end-to-end gain at ≈4–8%, not 1.3–1.8×. Kernel-level: a 3–5× reduction in HBM traffic on a bandwidth-bound kernel should give roughly a 3–5× kernel speed-up, not 1.3–1.8×, unless the kernel is not bandwidth-bound at those lengths — which is itself an important and unstated fact (at L=2,000 the fp16 score matrix is 8 MB and at L=4,000 it is 32 MB, both within H100's 50 MB L2, so the naive path's intermediate may not reach HBM at all). The chapter also asserts elsewhere that the KV working set 'exceeds L2 at any batch ≥ 1', which is true for KV but not for the attention score intermediate at these lengths — the two L2 facts need to be kept apart.
evidence: Attention FLOPs (full square) = 4·n_layers·L²·d = 4·80·L²·8192. L=2,000: 1.049e13; param-matmul = 2·70e9·2,000 = 2.8e14; attention share = 3.6%. L=4,000: 4.194e13 vs 5.6e14 → 7.0%. L=9,200: 2.219e14 vs 1.288e15 → 14.7% (matches the chapter's '≈15% of total'). Score-matrix bytes at fp16: L=2,000 → 8.0 MB; L=4,000 → 32.0 MB; H100 L2 = 50 MB.
root_cause: The chapter has a precise attention-share model in §3 but does not carry it into §5, where a bare speed-up multiplier is asserted; and it conflates the L2 residency of the KV working set with that of the attention score intermediate.
correction: State the referent ('attention-kernel throughput' or 'end-to-end request throughput'), and either derive the number from the chapter's own attention-share arithmetic or replace it with the derived bound (e.g. 'at 2,000–4,000 tokens attention is only 4–8% of forward FLOPs, so the end-to-end gain is bounded at roughly 4–8% even for a perfect attention kernel; the kernel-level gain is larger, and at these lengths the fp16 score matrix (8–32 MB) may fit in H100's 50 MB L2, which is why the benefit is length- and kernel-dependent').
acceptance_test: The §5 claim names its referent, and its magnitude is either derived from §3's attention-share numbers or explicitly bounded by them; the L2 discussion distinguishes the KV working set from the attention score intermediate.

page_hint: Ch15, 'The Optimization Decision Map', 'Two cautions' paragraph immediately below the table
quoted_clause: Second, the last two rows (P/D disaggregation, interconnect tuning) are the expensive, structural levers — they are worth testing only after the cheaper in-kernel and in-scheduler mechanisms have been measured and shown insufficient
observed: The parenthetical misidentifies the rows. The table's last two rows are row 7 ('multi-GPU execution dominated by communication' → interconnect/parallelism) and row 8 ('weight capacity or weight traffic limiting' → weight quantization). P/D disaggregation is row 6 ('prefill and decode interfering'). A reader who follows the reference lands on the weight-quantization row, which the chapter elsewhere explicitly calls a cheap, non-structural lever ('quantization is a candidate, not a win'), and misses the P/D row that carries the 'only after measuring' qualifier.
evidence: Table row order as printed: (1) high TTFT + compute saturated during prefill; (2) high TPOT/ITL + HBM bandwidth saturated; (3) KV exhaustion / low concurrency; (4) long-context attention dominated by memory traffic; (5) low GPU util, request-lifecycle mismatch; (6) prefill and decode interfering (contains 'chunked prefill ... then P/D disaggregation'); (7) multi-GPU execution dominated by communication; (8) weight capacity or weight traffic limiting.
root_cause: The sentence was written against an earlier row order (or from memory) and not re-checked after the table was edited.
correction: Replace 'the last two rows' with an explicit row identification, e.g. 'the P/D-disaggregation row and the interconnect-tuning row (rows 6 and 7) are the expensive, structural levers', or reorder the table so the structural levers are last.
acceptance_test: The sentence's row references resolve to the rows it describes when the table is read as printed.

page_hint: Ch15, 'The Optimization Decision Map', row 3 ('KV exhaustion / low concurrency')
quoted_clause: GQA/MQA (architecture-fixed — not a runtime lever; requires a re-checkpointed model), KV quantization, PagedAttention, context reduction, eviction/offload, prefix reuse | capacity vs transfer latency | lower per-request KV or offload
observed: 'Prefix reuse' is listed as a remedy for a memory-capacity bottleneck, but prefix caching does not reduce KV capacity demand: it eliminates prefill recomputation (a FLOP saving) while adding resident cached prefixes (a capacity cost). Listing it in the 'memory capacity' row invites the reader to believe that enabling prefix caching frees KV space for more concurrency, which is the opposite of its normal effect. The row's evidence column does list 'fragmentation', but the 'likely bottleneck' cell says only 'memory capacity', so the row conflates two distinct bottlenecks (raw capacity exhaustion vs fragmentation waste) that the chapter elsewhere insists on separating.
evidence: Chapter's own §3/§6: prefix caching stores additional KV blocks; the only capacity-reducing levers listed are KV quantization (2.62 → 1.31 MB/token), context reduction, eviction/offload, and GQA/MQA. §6's concurrency gain (17.5 → 35.0) is attributed to FP8 KV quantization, not to prefix reuse.
root_cause: The row was assembled as a list of 'KV-related techniques' rather than as a mapping from bottleneck to mechanism, which is the stated organizing principle of the map ('symptom → bottleneck → evidence → candidate mechanism chain').
correction: Remove 'prefix reuse' from the memory-capacity row (it belongs in the prefill-compute row, where it already appears as 'prefix caching'), and split the row's bottleneck cell into 'raw KV capacity' and 'KV fragmentation / allocator waste', assigning PagedAttention to the latter and KV quantization / context reduction / eviction-offload / GQA-MQA to the former.
acceptance_test: Every mechanism listed in a row of the map reduces the resource named in that row's 'likely bottleneck' cell; a reader can state which resource each listed mechanism relieves.

page_hint: Ch15 §6 (Architecture Consequence), final sentences of the paragraph beginning 'These choices together would change the basis of the throughput figure'
quoted_clause: 70,000 tok/s on one host would be ~124% MFU (a 2N-only check), so that figure is the *two-host* aggregate of the mini-case below (≈35,000 tok/s/host at its ~2× second-host factor) ... A fourth decision, raised by the mini-case (Ch11 §11.8) and not yet validated
observed: Two problems. (a) Cross-reference ambiguity: the same mini-case is called 'the mini-case below' and 'the mini-case (Ch11 §11.8)'. Chapter 11 precedes Chapter 15, so 'below' cannot refer to it; if Chapter 15 has its own end-of-chapter mini-case, the two references point at different objects and the reader cannot tell which supplies the 35,000 tok/s/host figure. (b) The phrase 'at its ~2× second-host factor' is uninterpretable: it could mean 'the second host contributes 2× the first' (total 3 hosts) or 'the factor is 2 hosts' (total 2 hosts). Only the latter reconciles with 2 × 35,000 = 70,000. (c) The imported figure conflicts with this chapter's own numbers: 35,000 tok/s/host ÷ 9,200 tok/req = 3.80 rps/host, versus §4's '~2 rps per host' admission capacity (17 slots ÷ 8.6 s = 1.98 rps) and §3's 19-host peak screen (19 × 1.98 = 37.6 rps). A two-host deployment at 3.8 rps/host covers ~7.6 rps, which is below even the canonical 10 rps average — so the mini-case's basis (workload level, context length, MFU) must be stated before its number can be used as the canonical deployment's throughput.
evidence: 35,000/9,200 = 3.80 rps/host; §4: 17/8.6 = 1.98 rps/host; §3: 6.5/0.35 = 18.6 → 19 hosts; 19 × 1.98 = 37.6 rps vs the 40 rps canonical peak. 2 hosts × 35,000 = 70,000 tok/s = 7.6 rps of prefill.
root_cause: A number imported from another chapter's worked example is used as a canonical-deployment figure without its workload level, context length, or efficiency assumption being carried along; and the cross-reference was written before the chapter's mini-case was placed.
correction: Resolve the reference to one object (state 'the mini-case in Ch 11 §11.8' or 'the mini-case at the end of this chapter', consistently), replace 'at its ~2× second-host factor' with the explicit arithmetic ('2 hosts × 35,000 tok/s/host'), and state the mini-case's workload level, context length, and implied MFU so the reader can see whether it is comparable with §3's 19-host peak screen and §4's ~2 rps/host admission capacity. If the mini-case is not the canonical workload, say so and stop using its per-host figure as the canonical range's lower endpoint (see CH15-01).
acceptance_test: Every cross-reference in §6 resolves to exactly one mini-case; the 70,000 tok/s figure is accompanied by its workload level and per-host MFU; and a reader can reconcile it with §3's 19-host screen and §4's ~2 rps/host without contradiction.

page_hint: Ch15 §6 (Architecture Consequence), decisions (3) and (4)
quoted_clause: (3) KV cache management via FP8 KV quantization ... plus length-based eviction of *inactive* prefix-cache entries (never truncation of an active request's context — active KV is offloaded or recomputed, per §5) ... A fourth decision, raised by the mini-case (Ch11 §11.8) and not yet validated, is to design the request-routing layer for KV cache affinity: when a user re-submits a request, routing to the same host avoids cache warm-up penalties and keeps p99 latency under the target SLO
observed: Decisions (3) and (4) are in direct conflict as written. Decision (3) evicts inactive prefix-cache entries by length; decision (4) relies on those same cached prefixes surviving so that an affinity-routed request finds a warm prefix. If the eviction policy removes the user's prefix, affinity routing yields no cache-warm-up benefit and the fourth decision's stated benefit ('keeps p99 latency under the target SLO') evaporates. The chapter is careful elsewhere to distinguish eviction of inactive prefixes from truncation of active context (§5), but it does not notice that its own two recommendations pull in opposite directions on the same objects.
evidence: §5: '(a) Evicting an idle/inactive prefix-cache entry — a cached prefix not currently in service — is safe, because no active request depends on it and it can be recomputed on reuse.' §6 decision (3) selects length-based eviction of exactly those entries; §6 decision (4) selects affinity routing to preserve exactly those entries.
root_cause: The two decisions were derived independently (one from the KV-capacity analysis, one from the mini-case) and never reconciled, although they govern the same cache objects.
correction: State the interaction and resolve it: either (i) make eviction affinity-aware (evict by (length, affinity) so that a user's likely-to-be-reused prefix is retained), or (ii) scope decision (4) to prefixes that survive the eviction policy, or (iii) note that decision (4) is conditional on decision (3)'s eviction policy and mark it as unresolved. Also state that the p99 benefit of affinity routing is unvalidated (as the text already does) and that it competes with the capacity freed by eviction.
acceptance_test: §6 contains an explicit statement of how the eviction policy and the affinity-routing policy interact, and no reader can apply both as written and expect the affinity benefit to materialize.

page_hint: Ch15 §4 (Measurement, final paragraph) vs §6 (Architecture Consequence, decision (2))
quoted_clause: §4: 'beyond batch‑4 the p95 latency typically rises (implying a knee near batch 4)' ... §6: '(2) continuous batching, with the maximum decode-step batch granularity chosen empirically from the measured goodput/latency knee ... (a max batch size of 8 requests per decode step — an [ILLUSTRATIVE] configuration, not the recommendation; the knee must be measured on the target stack)'
observed: The chapter's own §4 locates the goodput/latency knee near batch 4, and §6 then illustrates the chosen maximum decode-step batch as 8 — above the knee it just identified — while simultaneously saying the value must be chosen from the measured knee. Both numbers are labelled illustrative, but they are the chapter's only two statements about where the knee is, and they disagree. A reader who takes either at face value gets a different operating point, and the architecture-consequence section is where the reader expects the chapter's own analysis to have converged.
evidence: §4: 'beyond batch‑4 the p95 latency typically rises (implying a knee near batch 4)'; §6: 'a max batch size of 8 requests per decode step'. The §4 sweep is (1, 4, 16, 32), so 8 is not even one of the measured points.
root_cause: The illustrative configuration in §6 was chosen independently of the illustrative knee in §4, and neither was reconciled with the other or with the §4 sweep grid.
correction: Make §6's illustrative value consistent with §4 (e.g. 'a maximum decode-step batch of 4–8 requests, with the value set by the measured knee; note that the §4 sweep grid (1, 4, 16, 32) should be extended to include the chosen value'), or drop the specific number from §6 and keep only the method. If 8 is retained, state why it is acceptable above the knee (e.g. as a hard cap on tail latency rather than an operating point).
acceptance_test: The illustrative batch size in §6 does not exceed the illustrative knee in §4 without an explicit justification, and the §4 sweep grid contains the value §6 recommends.

page_hint: Ch15, Fig 15.1 caption (FlashAttention), final sentences of the caption body
quoted_clause: Both paths still do Θ(L²) HBM element accesses (with d fixed) — the gain is a constant factor set by on-chip capacity (d²/M), not a lower order.
observed: The I/O-complexity statement is ambiguous in sign and loose in units. In the FlashAttention I/O analysis, the fused kernel's HBM traffic in the quadratic regime is Θ(L²d²/M) while the materialized path's is Θ(L²); the reduction factor is therefore M/d² (how much larger the on-chip budget is than d²), and d²/M is the retained fraction. Calling d²/M 'the gain' reads as a speed-up factor of 0.083 (i.e. a 12× reduction) to one reader and as a slowdown to another. The units are also inconsistent: d is a head dimension in elements while M is an SRAM size in bytes, so d²/M is not dimensionless unless element size is silently taken as 1. The caption's own scope note ('the exact number of K/V re-reads depends on the tile scheduling, sequence length, and SRAM size') is the right caveat, but it sits above a formula that states the opposite kind of certainty.
evidence: FlashAttention I/O analysis (Dao et al.): fused kernel Θ(Nd²/M) HBM accesses vs Θ(Nd + N²) for the materialized path; the quadratic-term ratio is M/d². With d = 128 and M ≈ 192 KB (H100 shared memory per SM), d²/M ≈ 0.083 in element units — an idealized bound, not a realized traffic reduction, which is why the chapter elsewhere quotes a measured 3–5×.
root_cause: The caption compresses a two-sided complexity statement into a single ambiguous symbol without stating which side is the numerator, and mixes element and byte units.
correction: State the comparison explicitly and in consistent units, e.g. 'the fused kernel's HBM traffic in the quadratic regime is Θ(L²d²/M) versus Θ(L²) for the materialized path — a reduction factor of M/d², where M is the on-chip (SRAM) budget and d the head dimension; with d = 128 and M ≈ 192 KB the idealized bound is ≈12×, while realized reductions are smaller (see §5) because the materialized path's traffic depends on the number of softmax passes and on tile scheduling.'
acceptance_test: A reader can state which of the two paths has more traffic, by what factor, and in what units, without re-reading the caption; the caption's idealized bound is reconciled with the 3–5× figure quoted in §5.

page_hint: Ch15 §7 (What We Still Don't Know), fourth bullet
quoted_clause: Can in‑flight KV cache compression (e.g. speculative decoding–guided pruning) reduce memory pressure without increasing p99 latency? Pruning less‑important key/value pairs based on attention weight magnitudes is promising, but the accuracy‑latency trade‑off needs empirical validation across model families.
observed: The parenthetical names a mechanism that does not correspond to any established technique: speculative decoding is a draft-and-verify acceleration method, and 'speculative decoding–guided pruning' is not a recognized KV-compression approach. The sentence's own description ('pruning less-important key/value pairs based on attention weight magnitudes') describes attention-score-based KV eviction/pruning (e.g. H2O-, SnapKV-, Quest-, PyramidKV-style methods), which is a different family with a different literature and different failure modes. As written, the bullet either invents a technique or mislabels a real one, and it carries no source. This is also the only bullet in §7 whose subject is not a genuine open question but a mis-citation.
evidence: The bullet's own explanatory clause describes attention-score-based KV pruning, not speculative decoding; no source is given for the named mechanism, in a section whose other bullets are framed as open questions rather than as claims.
root_cause: Two adjacent concepts (speculative decoding, covered at length in the 'Two Mechanisms' subsection, and attention-score-based KV pruning) were conflated when the bullet was drafted.
correction: Either name the concrete, citable family ('attention-score-based KV eviction/pruning — e.g. H2O- or SnapKV-style methods that retain the tokens with the highest accumulated attention weight — with a citation') and drop the speculative-decoding attribution, or, if there is a specific published speculative-decoding-guided KV-compression method, cite it by title, authors, and year. Keep the open question itself (accuracy vs p99 trade-off across model families), which is legitimate.
acceptance_test: The bullet names a mechanism that exists in the literature with a citation, and the mechanism's description matches the technique it names.

page_hint: Ch15 §3 (Worked Example), opening 'Canonical scenario' paragraph
quoted_clause: the canonical 80-layer, hidden-8192, full-MHA 70B reference model (a 70B-class dense FP16 model), 8×H100 host with 640 GB GPU memory
observed: The chapter's regime claims ('Decode is primarily memory-bandwidth constrained', 'HBM bandwidth saturated' in the decision map) depend on the host's HBM bandwidth, but the chunk never states the H100 variant or its bandwidth. 640 GB implies eight 80 GB parts, which covers both H100 SXM (3.35 TB/s) and H100 PCIe (2.0 TB/s) — a 1.68× difference that changes every bandwidth conclusion in the chapter, including the decode ceiling computed in CH15-02 (809 tok/s at SXM, ~485 tok/s at PCIe). The chapter also does not say whether the 8 GPUs are NVLinked.
evidence: H100 SXM: 80 GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s. H100 PCIe: 80 GB HBM2e, 2.0 TB/s. H100 NVL: 94 GB, 3.9 TB/s. The chunk's '640 GB GPU memory' is consistent with SXM or PCIe.
root_cause: The hardware specification is inherited from Chapter 8 by implication rather than stated where the bandwidth reasoning is actually performed.
correction: State the variant and its HBM bandwidth in the canonical-scenario paragraph (or add an explicit cross-reference to Chapter 8's canonical H100 specification), and note the interconnect (NVLink/NVSwitch) since §4's collective-measurement paragraph and the decision map's interconnect row depend on it.
acceptance_test: The canonical scenario paragraph names the H100 variant, its per-GPU HBM bandwidth, and the interconnect, so that every bandwidth figure in the chapter can be recomputed from the chapter alone.
